title: Animals matter
hook: Jewish law requires feeding your animals before yourself (Berakhot 40a)

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was fair work: pay on time, work with your strength. Did you do your one act before sundown? Today, the ones who work for us and can't ask for anything. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-seven.

Six-thirty in the morning. The coffee is brewing, your stomach is complaining, and the cat is sitting by the bowl, staring. Who eats first? It sounds like a question of manners, or of who complains loudest. The Talmud treats it as a question of law. In tractate Berakhot, the teacher Rav Yehudah says, in Rav's name, that a person may not eat until they have fed their animals. Today, why the rabbis put the cat's breakfast before yours, and what else the tradition says animals are owed.
screen: `WHO EATS FIRST?` → `NOT A QUESTION OF MANNERS.` → `THE ANIMALS, SAYS THE TALMUD.`

segments.voice: Turn it four ways. First, the order of a verse. The rule comes from a line in Deuteronomy, read as part of the Shema: "And I will give grass in thy fields for thy cattle, and thou shalt eat and be satisfied." The rabbis noticed the order. The cattle are given grass, and then you eat. They made the verse's order into the household's order. Second, the Torah's other rules. Don't muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain; it may eat from what it works. Rest on the Sabbath includes your ox and your donkey. If your enemy's donkey is lying under its load, help lift it. The rabbis gathered teachings like these under a name: tza'ar ba'alei chayim, the suffering of living things, and they treated causing needless suffering to animals as forbidden. Third, a story about a teacher. In tractate Bava Metzia, a calf being led to slaughter runs to Rabbi Judah the Prince, hides its head in his robe, and cries. He tells it: go, for this you were created. The Talmud says suffering came upon him for that, because he showed no compassion. One day, his housekeeper is about to sweep out a litter of small animals. He stops her, quoting a psalm: "his tender mercies are over all his works." And the Talmud says his suffering ended. Fourth, what it means. Jewish law permits eating meat, with rules. But in these texts, an animal is never a mere thing. Its hunger comes first at breakfast, and its fear in a doorway matters.
screen: `GRASS FOR THE CATTLE, THEN YOU EAT.` · `THE SUFFERING OF LIVING THINGS.` · `A CALF HIDES IN A ROBE.` · `HIS MERCIES OVER ALL HIS WORKS.` · then, large: `ANIMALS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed an animal first. If you have a pet, plan to fill its bowl before you eat your next meal, and to notice it eating. If you don't, there's still a way: a bird feeder, a dish of water on a hot step, a neighbor's dog you could greet, or simply some care with the small life around you. Sit, and breathe. Let one animal you'll meet today come to mind. Notice its hunger, its tiredness, its fear. Choose one small kindness you can give it before you look after yourself. The bell holds the time.
Animals matter. The rabbis' phrase is tza'ar ba'alei chayim, the suffering of living things, and they put an animal's meal before your own. Today's word.
Your line: animals first. Today, at your next meal, feed or tend to one animal before you take your first bite. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish law codes rule, following Berakhot 40a, that a person feeds their animals before eating, and tza'ar ba'alei chayim is studied as a principle of Jewish law.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to animals.
what it means: an animal's need is a duty: fed before you eat, rested on the Sabbath, spared needless suffering.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 40a reads the order of Deuteronomy 11:15; Bava Metzia 85a tells of the calf and Psalm 145:9.

notes: Berakhot 40a: Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav, from Deuteronomy 11:15; confirm attribution.
Deuteronomy 11:15 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm. 'read as part of the Shema' refers to the second paragraph; confirm.
Exodus 23:5 (the enemy's donkey under its load), Exodus 23:12 / Deuteronomy 5:14 (Sabbath rest for ox and donkey), Deuteronomy 25:4 (ox not muzzled) are paraphrased.

Tza'ar ba'alei chayim described as a rabbinic principle forbidding needless suffering; the question of whether it is biblical or rabbinic is debated and the script avoids deciding it. Confirm the wording.
Bava Metzia 85a: the calf and the weasels/small animals story, retold; confirm details (the housekeeper sweeping, Psalm 145:9).
